subject: Biology
title: Biodiversity and Conservation
summary: Biodiversity (a term popularised by Edward Wilson) exists at three levels: genetic, species and ecological diversity. About 1.5 million species have been described; estimates of the total range up to about 7 million (Robert May).
India has only 2.4% of the world's land area but 8.1% of its species diversity — one of 12 mega-diversity countries. Diversity is highest in the tropics and falls towards the poles.

Alexander von Humboldt's species–area relationship: species richness rises with area, up to a limit. Loss of biodiversity is driven by the 'Evil Quartet': habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions.
Conservation is in situ (hotspots, protected areas, sacred groves) or ex situ (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation).

formulas.name: Levels of biodiversity
formulas.formula: genetic (Rauwolfia vomitoria — reserpine variation; India has 50,000+ strains of rice and 1000 varieties of mango);  species (Western Ghats have more amphibian species than Eastern Ghats);  ecological (India's deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows)

formulas.name: Global species proportions
formulas.formula: more than 70% of recorded species are animals; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms) are about 22%;  among animals insects are 70% (7 of every 10 animals)

formulas.name: Species–area relationship
formulas.formula: log S = log C + Z log A  (S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope, C = Y-intercept)
formulas.note: For very large areas like whole continents, Z is much steeper (0.6–1.2).

formulas.name: Z values
formulas.formula: Z ≈ 0.1–0.2 for small areas regardless of taxonomic group or region;  frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests across continents: Z ≈ 1.15

formulas.name: Why tropics are richer
formulas.formula: long evolutionary time (undisturbed for millions of years);  less seasonal, more constant environment (niche specialisation);  more solar energy → higher productivity

formulas.name: Evil Quartet
formulas.formula: habitat loss and fragmentation (Amazon rain forest — 'lungs of the planet');  over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon);  alien species invasions (Nile perch in Lake Victoria; Parthenium, Lantana, Eichhornia; African catfish Clarias gariepinus);  co-extinctions (host fish and its parasites; plant–pollinator)

formulas.name: Recent extinctions
formulas.formula: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia);  three subspecies of tiger: Bali, Javan, Caspian;  last 500 years: 784 extinctions (IUCN 2004)
formulas.note: The IUCN Red List (Red Data Book) records threatened species in categories such as critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable.

formulas.name: Rivet popper hypothesis
formulas.formula: Paul Ehrlich: the ecosystem is an aeroplane and species are rivets — losing a few may not matter, but losing key ones (on the wings) threatens the whole system

formulas.name: Biodiversity hotspots
formulas.formula: high species richness + high endemism;  34 hotspots worldwide (less than 2% of land area);  India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya

formulas.name: Protected areas in India
formulas.formula: 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 wildlife sanctuaries;  Ramsar sites protect wetlands of international importance

formulas.name: Sacred groves
formulas.formula: Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghats (Karnataka, Maharashtra), Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar (Madhya Pradesh)

formulas.name: Ex situ conservation
formulas.formula: zoos, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks;  cryopreservation of gametes (−196 °C);  in vitro fertilisation;  tissue culture propagation;  seed banks

formulas.name: International efforts
formulas.formula: Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro (1992) — Convention on Biological Diversity;  World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg (2002) — reduce biodiversity loss by 2010

examples.title: Doubling the area
examples.problem: With Z = 0.2, by what factor does species richness rise if the area doubles?

examples.title: India's share
examples.problem: What share of world land area and species does India have?
examples.solution: 2.4% of the land area and 8.1% of the species diversity — a mega-diversity country with over 45,000 plant and twice as many animal species recorded.

examples.title: Lake Victoria
examples.problem: How did the Nile perch affect Lake Victoria?
examples.solution: Introduced into the lake, it led to the extinction of more than 200 species of native cichlid fish — an alien species invasion.

examples.title: Co-extinction
examples.solution: When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique parasites also become extinct. Similarly, a plant and its obligate pollinator depend on each other.

examples.title: Why conserve biodiversity?
examples.problem: Give the three types of arguments for conservation.
examples.solution: Narrowly utilitarian (food, fibre, medicines — over 25% of drugs come from plants), broadly utilitarian (ecosystem services; the Amazon forest produces about 20% of total O₂ by photosynthesis) and ethical (every species has intrinsic value).

topics.title: Number of species
topics.explain: IUCN (2004) put described plants and animals at slightly more than 1.5 million. Robert May estimated about 7 million species globally. Many more species remain undiscovered, especially among prokaryotes, insects and tropical species.

topics.title: Importance of species diversity
topics.explain: Communities with more species tend to be more stable — David Tilman's long-term plot experiments showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in biomass and higher productivity.

topics.title: Amazon rain forest
topics.explain: It harbours probably millions of species, including more than 40,000 plants, 3000 fish, 1300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates.

topics.title: Biopiracy and bioprospecting
topics.explain: Bioprospecting is exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance. Nations rich in biodiversity can benefit by bioprospecting.

topics.title: Loss rate
topics.explain: Current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1000 times faster than in pre-human times; 12% of birds, 23% of mammals, 32% of amphibians and 31% of gymnosperms are facing the threat of extinction. Ecologists warn of a sixth mass extinction.

topics.title: Effects of biodiversity loss
topics.explain: Decline in plant production, lower resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought, and increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles.

ratta: log S = log C + Z log A;  Z 0.1–0.2 (small areas), 0.6–1.2 (continents).
Evil Quartet: habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien invasions, co-extinction.
34 hotspots;  India: Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya.
